input.question: Why a flight going East to West takes longer than exact same flight going West to East?
input.ground_truth: Because over a given part of the earth the wind moves predominantly in one direction . Hence one way the plane is flying into the wind and one it's flying with the wind. At the altitude of airliners the wind speeds constitute a noticeable fraction of the nominal speed of the aircraft - hence the difference. EDIT: I should have added that for this reason I wouldn't expect to see the affect you're describing on a generally north-south routing (eg london - cape town).

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why a flight going East to West takes longer than exact same flight going West to East?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine the Earth is like a big, round ball that spins around. The Earth spins from west to east, which means it’s always moving a little bit that way.

When you fly east (the same way the Earth spins), you get a little “push” from the Earth’s spinning, just like when you run on a moving walkway at the airport—it helps you go faster. So flying east can be a tiny bit faster.

But when you fly west (against the way the Earth spins), it’s like running the other way on the moving walkway—it’s a little harder, so you go a bit slower.

Because of this, a flight going west to east (with the spin) is usually a little bit faster, so the same trip going east to west (against the spin) takes a tiny bit longer. But for most flights, the difference is very, very small—just a few minutes!
